clinicalPearls: Caused by biallelic variants in TYRP1 and classically produces 'rufous' (red) oculocutaneous albinism, best characterised in southern African populations.
Affected individuals typically have reddish-bronze or ginger-red skin and hair with blue-to-hazel irides, reflecting a shift away from brown-black eumelanin.
Ocular involvement is often milder than in OCA1 or OCA2, but nystagmus, foveal hypoplasia and reduced acuity can still occur.
TYRP1 acts downstream in eumelanin synthesis, so its loss reduces dark eumelanin while relatively preserving red-yellow phaeomelanin.
Because features can be subtle, OCA3 is easily under-recognised and may be mistaken for a constitutional red-haired phenotype.
Photoprotection and cutaneous malignancy surveillance remain important despite the comparatively mild appearance.
Inheritance is autosomal recessive; molecular confirmation and genetic counselling are advised.
reference.pathophysiology: OCA3 arises from loss-of-function variants in TYRP1 on chromosome 9, encoding tyrosinase-related protein 1. TYRP1 functions within the melanosome to stabilise tyrosinase and to catalyse a step in the eumelanin (brown-black pigment) synthetic pathway. Deficient TYRP1 activity therefore selectively curtails eumelanin production while red-yellow phaeomelanin is relatively spared, generating the characteristic rufous colouring of skin and hair. Because some pigment is retained and the ocular pathway is less severely disrupted than in tyrosinase-negative albinism, ophthalmic features such as foveal hypoplasia, nystagmus and chiasmal misrouting are variable and sometimes mild.
additionalDifferentials: Oculocutaneous albinism type 2 (OCA2 gene) — pigment-permitting phenotype.
Constitutional red-hair phenotype due to MC1R variants without albinism.
Other OCA subtypes such as OCA6 and OCA7.
Syndromic albinism — Hermansky-Pudlak and Chediak-Higashi syndromes.
additionalInvestigations: Ophthalmological assessment including acuity, nystagmus and iris transillumination.
Optical coherence tomography for foveal hypoplasia.
Visual evoked potentials for chiasmal misrouting.
Molecular genetic testing of TYRP1 within an oculocutaneous albinism panel.
Dermatological review and cutaneous malignancy surveillance.
redFlags: Suspicious, changing or non-healing cutaneous lesions indicating skin malignancy.
Unusually severe visual impairment prompting reassessment for another OCA subtype.
Systemic features such as a bleeding tendency or recurrent infections suggesting syndromic albinism.
reference.prognosis: The condition is generally mild, with a normal lifespan and often only modest visual impairment. As with all albinism, cumulative ultraviolet exposure raises the risk of skin cancer, mitigated by photoprotection and surveillance.
pitfalls: Dismissing the phenotype as ordinary red hair rather than recognising albinism.
Assuming ocular features are always mild and omitting formal visual assessment.
Relying on appearance alone rather than confirming the subtype with TYRP1 testing.
Neglecting skin-cancer prevention because pigmentation looks relatively preserved.
management: No curative treatment; lifelong photoprotection with broad-spectrum sunscreen, protective clothing and sun avoidance despite the comparatively mild rufous phenotype
Regular dermatological surveillance with dermoscopy for cutaneous malignancy
Optimisation of vision with refractive correction, tints for photophobia and low-vision aids where nystagmus and reduced acuity are present
Orthoptic assessment and management of nystagmus and strabismus when present
Genetic counselling for autosomal recessive TYRP1-related disease with testing of at-risk relatives
